newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba says no more than 10 deaths from dengue fever.
newsitem.headline: Cuba says no more than 10 deaths from dengue fever.

text.p: Cuban Health Minister Carlos Dotres has said not more than 10 people have died in an outbreak of the tropical disease dengue fever in the eastern city of Santiago de Cuba in the past six weeks.

Dotres, speaking late on Monday to a group of Spanish university rectors in remarks made available to Spanish journalists on Tuesday, said the outbreak was now controlled. He added that authorities expected the disease to be completely eliminated in two to three weeks time.
Dotres said the number of deaths was at most 10, all of them adults, but did not give an exact figure. He added some of these deaths had been among people suffering prior chronic illnesses.
Some foreign media last month reported a higher death toll in the outbreak of the mosquito-carried disease that began in Cuba's second city in May.

Cuban health officials said in mid-June there had been about 730 cases of the disease. Dotres did not give an updated figure for the number of cases reported since the outbreak began, but stressed the disease had only affected Santiago de Cuba.

Dengue, transmitted by the Aedes Aegypti mosquito, causes headaches and body aches, high fever and a rash and usually lasts for about one week. In its most serious form, which is rare, it can cause haemorrhages and can be fatal.
Cuban authorities have noted the disease is common in parts of southern United States, central America and the Caribbean.

The outbreak of dengue in Santiago de Cuba has been the first of the disease in Cuba since epidemics in 1981 and 1977-78. The 1981 epidemic involved several hundred thousand cases and caused 150 deaths.
Measures to counter the disease focus on eradicating the mosquito that carries it, by fumigating and also eliminating stagnant pools of water where the mosquito breeds.
